The Greenback flounder (Rhombosolea tapirina) is a pleuronectiform flatfish endemic to the coastal waters of southern Australia and Tasmania, where it supports a moderately important commercial and recreational fishery. Field surveys and laboratory rearing studies have provided a detailed picture of its life-history schedule. At a stable water temperature of 16.6 °C [T = 16.6 °C], the embryonic period is relatively brief: hatching of the pelagic egg occurs after 7.5 days [ab = 7.5 days], a duration consistent with the rapid developmental rates typical of temperate marine teleost larvae. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva, or prolarva, is minute, with a wet weight at birth of only 0.00037 grams [Wwb = 0.00037 grams]. This lecithotrophic larva relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during its first days, undergoing organogenesis and retinal differentiation before the mouth opens and first exogenous feeding becomes possible. The hatchling mass is among the lowest recorded for pleuronectid flatfishes of comparable adult body size, reflecting the small dimensions of the transparent, yolk-laden egg from which it emerges.

As the yolk-sac larva exhausts its endogenous reserves and initiates exogenous feeding, growth proceeds rapidly through the planktonic larval phase. The pre-metamorphic larva, now an actively feeding ichthyoplanktonic organism, drifts in coastal currents until reaching a developmental threshold that triggers the dramatic allometric shifts associated with metamorphosis. During this larval-juvenile transition, the left eye migrates, the body plan reorganizes, and the pelagic larva settles to the benthos as a post-metamorphic juvenile or fingerling. Comparative growth data indicate that the onset of sexual maturation—marked by gonad maturation and vitellogenesis onset in females—occurs when individuals attain a total length at puberty of 20 centimeters [Lp = 20 centimeters]. This length threshold is reached after a growing period of roughly one to two years, depending on local thermal conditions and prey availability. At this same developmental milestone, the wet weight at puberty has been estimated at 133 grams [Wwp = 133 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions fitted to field-caught specimens across the species' geographic range.

Reproductive investment in female Greenback flounder scales with body size in a pattern typical of iteroparous teleosts. The ultimate female wet weight, representing the asymptotic body mass attained by the largest individuals in the population, has been estimated at 1480 grams [Wwi = 1480 grams]. This value, together with the corresponding ultimate total length of 45 centimeters [Li = 45 centimeters], places Rhombosolea tapirina at the upper end of the size spectrum within the pleuronectid genus Rhombosolea. Large, old females contribute disproportionately to population fecundity, as fecundity scales positively with length and mass in most flatfishes. These maximum size records were obtained from long-term commercial catch samples and validated by museum specimen measurements, providing robust benchmarks for life-history comparisons. At 45 centimeters [Li = 45 centimeters], this size is rarely observed in contemporary fisheries, likely due to size-selective harvest pressure that truncates the age structure and reduces the number of individuals reaching their full growth potential.

The species' longevity has been investigated through otolith-based ageing studies and tag-recapture programs conducted across Tasmanian and South Australian waters. Under the same thermal conditions that characterize the rearing experiments for early life stages, maintained at a water temperature of 16.6 °C [T = 16.6 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan is approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years]. This value aligns with the moderate longevity observed in other temperate flatfishes of similar body size, representing a life-history strategy that balances annual reproductive output against the cumulative mortality risks of the demersal adult habitat. Sexually mature individuals, beginning with those that have attained puberty at 20 centimeters [Lp = 20 centimeters] total length, participate in annual spawning migrations to inshore nursery grounds. The age structure of wild populations suggests that few individuals survive beyond eight years, and senescence, marked by a decline in reproductive condition and a gradual loss of body condition, typically manifests during the ninth or tenth year.

Ecologically, the Greenback flounder occupies estuarine and coastal soft-sediment habitats, where it feeds predominantly on polychaetes, small crustaceans, and bivalve siphons. The large asymptotic mass of 1480 grams [Wwi = 1480 grams] and the substantial investment in gonadal tissue that this body size supports enable females to produce large numbers of pelagic eggs during each spawning event. Interestingly, when considering the transition from the prolarva stage to sexual maturity, the increase in body mass is remarkable: from 0.00037 grams [Wwb = 0.00037 grams] at birth to 133 grams [Wwp = 133 grams] at puberty, representing a gain of several orders of magnitude over a relatively short developmental period. The flat body morphology and cryptic coloration of the benthic juvenile and adult stages provide effective concealment from piscine predators, contributing to a survivorship schedule that, combined with a maximum lifespan of 10 years [am = 10 years] at 16.6 °C [T = 16.6 °C], defines the species as a moderately K-selected marine teleost within the constraints of a productive temperate estuary ecosystem.
